There's a word I find quietly astonishing: "meanwhile." It slips into sentences without ceremony, yet it carries an entire universe inside it. Every time someone says "meanwhile," they're acknowledging that right now, at this very moment, countless other lives are unfolding—someone is locking a bicycle outside a bakery in Lisbon, someone is teaching a child to whistle, someone is sitting alone in a hospital corridor rehearsing difficult news.

We live our lives as protagonists, naturally. Our own worries have surround sound; other people's are silent films we glimpse through windows. But "meanwhile" is a small act of humility. It admits that the world doesn't pause when we close our eyes.

I think about this most on trains. A train car is a temporary anthology of unfinished stories: the woman annotating a manuscript, the teenager nervously refreshing his phone, the man asleep with his mouth open, trusting strangers completely. In forty minutes, everyone will scatter to different neighborhoods, different decades of their lives, and likely never see each other again. Yet for this stretch of track, they share warmth, light, the gentle sway of the carriage.

Maybe that's what cities are—millions of "meanwhiles" stacked vertically, pressed side by side. And maybe kindness is just the willingness to remember it. To let the stranger merge into traffic. To be patient with the slow cashier. To understand that behind every tired face is a whole weather system of private joys and griefs.

The world is enormous. "Meanwhile" is how we hold that enormity gently.
